source: Lee, Oh, Kim, Shin, Tack (2025) ReVISE: Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ICML)
finding: ReVISE adds a special token after each answer: [eos] means stop, [refine] means revise. Trained in two stages with preference learning (DPO): first verification, then correction. The model learns when to refine.
numbers: Method: one reasoning path per sample for preference pairs, about 50,000 generations in total. Models Llama-3.2-1B and Llama-3.1-8B, trained on GSM8K, MATH, MBPP.
limits: Small models (1B to 8B) only. Trained per dataset. Gains are in single digits.
agent_relevance: This is the learned S5 trigger: a model-internal stop-or-refine decision. Our agent cannot train, but it shows the trigger can be one binary decision on the answer.

source: Lee, Oh, Kim, Shin, Tack (2025) ReVISE: Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ICML) - main table
finding: ReVISE beats few-shot CoT, SFT, RFT and STaR+ on math at equal training data. Maj@1 is already best before any voting.
numbers: Llama-3.2-1B GSM8K Maj@1 28.1 vs RFT 26.2, SFT 22.1; Maj@5 32.8 vs STaR+ 29.9. MATH-500 Maj@1 13.4 vs 12.6. Llama-3.1-8B GSM8K Maj@1 61.6 vs 59.2 (STaR+); Maj@5 69.2 vs 65.3. MATH-500 Maj@1 33.6 vs RFT 30.8; Maj@5 37.6 vs 35.6. Few-shot CoT 8B: 56.7 GSM8K, 23.4 MATH-500.
limits: Gains over the strongest baseline are about 1 to 4 points. No confidence intervals in Table 1. MATH-500 1B scores are very low (13.4).
agent_relevance: A learned refine trigger gives a few points. It does not remove the need for a real check; it is a cheap prior.

source: Lee, Oh, Kim, Shin, Tack (2025) ReVISE: Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ICML) - code and verification quality
finding: ReVISE also helps on code. Its own verification signal predicts correctness better than a separately trained verifier.
numbers: MBPP Pass@1 (Llama-3.2-1B): ReVISE 33.1, STaR+ 30.7, SFT 30.0, RFT 29.6, few-shot 24.5. GSM8K AUROC of self-verification: ReVISE 76.0 vs V-STaR verifier 69.5. Without curriculum AUROC 71; with two-stage curriculum 76. Two-stage curriculum final accuracy 22.6 -> 28.1.
limits: AUROC 76 is far from reliable. Stage-2 training slightly lowers verification accuracy (authors note forgetting).
agent_relevance: Even a trained intrinsic verifier is only about 0.76 AUROC. Treat the trigger as a hint (G4); let code checks decide when a check exists.

source: Lee, Oh, Kim, Shin, Tack (2025) ReVISE: Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ICML) - confidence-weighted voting and test-time scaling
finding: Summing the model's own [eos]-vs-[refine] confidence over identical answers beats plain majority vote and scales with samples.
numbers: GSM8K 1B ablation: confidence-weighted 33.9 vs unweighted majority 33.2 and another scheme 32.7. Maj@64 (Table 8): ReVISE 37.7 vs best baseline 33.2. At N=2 plain majority gives no gain; confidence-weighted does. Iterative refinement: 4.0 point gain after refinement on MATH-500 (8B).
limits: Voting gain vs plain majority is under 1 point in the ablation. Extra refinement rounds help but plateau (Figure 8).
agent_relevance: Weak support for weighting votes by a calibrated verifier confidence; our G5 keeps selection in code.

source: Lee, Oh, Kim, Shin, Tack (2025) ReVISE: Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ICML) - comparison with SCoRe and DPO
finding: On Gemma-2-2B MATH-500, ReVISE matches SCoRe at about 1/30 of the training generations. Plain DPO without the refine token is worse.
numbers: MATH-500 Gemma-2-2B: zero-shot 16.8, SFT 17.6, RFT 18.6, SCoRe 23.0, ReVISE 23.2, +1 iteration 24.2, +2 iterations 25.8. SCoRe about 1.5M generations (3,000 steps x batch 512) vs ReVISE 50,000. Removing DPO loss: -10.3 points. ReVISE beats a DPO baseline by 22.7 (GSM8K) and 10.8 (MATH-500) in Table 5.
limits: SCoRe numbers are copied from the SCoRe paper because no code was open. No replication by others found in this pass.
agent_relevance: A 0.2 gap over SCoRe is not meaningful. The real gain is cost, which matters little for a scaffold-only agent.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR)
finding: Without oracle labels, asking a model to review and fix its answer lowers reasoning accuracy. Earlier gains came from using the ground-truth label to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7 over two rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K.
quote: after self-correction, the accuracies of all models drop across all benchmarks
limits: Prompted intrinsic self-correction only; says nothing about trained correctors. Old GPT-3.5/GPT-4 versions.
agent_relevance: Evidence behind G1 and G2: never revise from opinion alone. It is the baseline ReVISE and SCoRe try to beat.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet - debate vs self-consistency
finding: Re-running multi-agent debate (Du et al.) on the full GSM8K test set, not 100 items, shows it is no better than self-consistency at equal numbers of responses.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K: standard 76.7; self-consistency with 3 responses 82.5; debate round 1 (6 responses) 83.2 vs self-consistency 6: 85.3; debate round 2 (9 responses) 83.0 vs self-consistency 9: 88.2.
limits: One model, one dataset.
agent_relevance: Supports G9 (no debate): equal-cost voting wins.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
finding: SFT on correction traces fails because of distribution mismatch and collapse to not correcting. Two-stage multi-turn online RL on the model's own traces gives clearly positive intrinsic self-correction.
numbers: Absolute self-correction gain of 15.6% on MATH and 9.1% on HumanEval over the base Gemini models. Earlier SFT and STaR-style baselines show self-correction deltas from about -11 to +2 points.
quote: first approach to attain significantly positive intrinsic self-correction
limits: Gemini models, closed. No public code (ReVISE says so). Compute is large (RL).
agent_relevance: Lesson: train on the model's own first attempts. For us: S5 should be fed the actual failing output from S4, not a fixed template (matches G2).

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han, Zhang (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs (TACL)
finding: Survey of prior work. Self-correction works only when reliable external feedback exists, or after fine-tuning on large data. No prior work shows success from prompted self-generated feedback on general tasks.
numbers: Three research questions defined: RQ1 inherent ability, RQ2 with external information, RQ3 versus other methods. Many studies use oracle labels, weak initial prompts, or ignore cost.
quote: no prior work shows reliable evidence of successful self-correction with in-context learning
limits: Literature review, no new experiments. Cutoff early 2024.
agent_relevance: The bottleneck is feedback generation, not the fix. Matches G2: show real failing output, located by code.

source: Tyen, Mansoor, Carbune, Chen, Mak (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (Findings ACL)
finding: On BIG-Bench Mistake (2,186 PaLM 2 CoT traces with the first logical error labeled), all tested LLMs are poor at finding mistakes. Given the location, they fix it well.
numbers: Best model GPT-4 reaches 52.87 overall mistake-location accuracy with direct step-level prompting. With oracle location and backtracking, word sorting: 23.53% of originally wrong traces become right, 11.11% of originally right traces become wrong. Random-location baseline gains are much smaller. About 85% of traces have wrong final answers.
limits: Traces from one model (PaLM 2 Unicorn); BIG-Bench style tasks. Oracle location is unavailable in real use.
agent_relevance: Core evidence for G2: finding is the weak step, fixing is strong. Code (tests, mutation, held-out inputs) should locate the error, then the model fixes.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) - trained mistake finder
finding: A small mistake-finding classifier trained on out-of-domain data beats few-shot prompting of a large model.
numbers: Reported as proof of concept; exact per-task values not recorded here.
limits: Proof of concept only.
agent_relevance: A trained verifier can beat prompting, the ReVISE idea, but we cannot train.

source: Zhang, Khalifa, Logeswaran, Lee, Lee, Wang (2024) Small Language Models Need Strong Verifiers to Self-Correct Reasoning (ACL Findings)
finding: Split self-correction into verify then refine. A fine-tuned refiner (SCORE) works with a strong verifier but not with a weak self-verifier trained on the model's own outputs.
numbers: LLaMA-2-13B-chat and Gemma-7b-it, five math and commonsense datasets. With a GPT-4 verifier, average gain 14.6% over the original model. With a weak self-trained verifier, self-correction struggles.
limits: Small models only. The strong verifier is GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Who decides when to refine matters more than how. A weak trigger cancels a good refiner. Use code or a stronger judge as the S4 trigger.

source: Qu, Zhang, Kumar, Yang, Kolter, Salakhutdinov, Kumar (2024) Recursive Introspection (RISE): Teaching Language Model Agents How to Self-Improve
finding: RISE fine-tunes a model with iterative on-policy data to improve over several turns, then majority-votes across turns. Performance rises with each turn.
numbers: GSM8K: +8.2% for LLaMa3-8B, +6.6% for Mistral-7B using their own data; +17.7% for LLaMa2-7B over other methods.
limits: Fine-tuned per task. Paper notes strong proprietary models do not improve sequentially without training.
agent_relevance: Sequential self-improvement is a trained skill, not a prompt trick. Without training keep rounds at 2 or fewer (our S5 limit).

source: Ma et al. (2025) S2R: Teaching LLMs to Self-verify and Self-correct via Reinforcement Learning
finding: With only 3.1k self-verify/self-correct SFT samples, then outcome-level and process-level RL, both skills improve.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B: 51.0% -> 81.6% average accuracy (MATH500 +32.2, GSM8K +34.3 points over base). Outcome RL mainly raises error recall and correct precision; process RL raises overall verification accuracy. Some transfer to out-of-domain tasks such as FOLIO.
limits: Math-focused 7B model. Base starts weak, so part of the gain is format and length.
agent_relevance: Verification skill can be trained cheaply, but not by us. Error recall vs correct precision is a useful measure for any trigger.

source: Stechly, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: An Analysis of Iterative Prompting for Reasoning Problems
finding: On graph coloring (100 instances), GPT-4 self-critique makes results worse. A sound external verifier helps, but the content of the feedback does not matter.
numbers: No-backprompt baseline 16%. GPT-4 as its own verifier: 1 of 100 correct. Sound verifier: near 40%; binary feedback vs one error vs all errors differ insignificantly. In 39 of 40 chains where an optimal coloring appeared, the GPT verifier hallucinated same-colored edges. Scoring a hit at any point in the chain also gives about 40%.
limits: One task (graph coloring), GPT-4 2023.
agent_relevance: Supports G10 and G4: the gain comes from an external check that stops and re-samples, not from the model's critique. Resample with a code stopper.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: On Game of 24, graph coloring and STRIPS planning, LLM self-verification is poor, with false positives and false negatives that sink the loop.
numbers: Game of 24: of equations that equal 24, the model marks 79.1% as correct, yet evaluates 81.6% of them to 24, so some correctly evaluated ones are still marked wrong. A verification table shows overall accuracy 87.0% (3567/4100) with false positive rate 10.4% and false negative rate 20.7% in one setting; other subsets have false negative rates above 95%.
limits: Synthetic formal tasks. Table cell-to-setting mapping from text extraction may be imprecise.
agent_relevance: Verifier errors correlate with generator errors. Reinforces G3 and G5: verify with code or held-out checks.

source: Weng et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Better Reasoners with Self-Verification (Findings EMNLP)
finding: Backward verification: mask a condition in the question, plug a candidate answer in, and check whether the model recovers the masked value. Pick the candidate that recovers the most conditions.
numbers: Gains larger on arithmetic reasoning (average 1.67 / 2.84 points across two settings) than other reasoning tasks (0.62 / 0.78). New best result on six of eight datasets. More masked conditions helps. Works with 2-shot prompts.
limits: Gains are small and come from selecting among sampled candidates, not from repair.
agent_relevance: A label-free model-side check that reconstructs a given. A cheap S8 variant when no code check exists, small gains.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback (NeurIPS)
finding: One LLM generates, critiques and refines in a loop. Big gains on subjective or metric-graded tasks, small gains on math.
numbers: GPT-4 code optimization 27.3 -> 36.0 (+8.7 absolute). Math reasoning gain is described as modest; authors say the model cannot reliably detect an error in a consistent-looking chain. Appendix: Self-Correction 45.9% vs Self-Refine 55.7% on GSM8K with GPT-3.
quote: The modest performance gains in Math Reasoning can be traced back to the inability to accurately identify whether there is any error
limits: Not matched for compute; Huang et al. later argued math gains rely on oracle stopping.
agent_relevance: Refinement works where quality is gradable. For single-answer problems use a code check instead.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing (ICLR)
finding: Tools (search, code interpreter) produce the critique. Gains grow with model size; without tool feedback self-correction is unreliable.
numbers: TabMWP gains of +4.7, +9.4, +16.0 for 7B, 13B, 70B models. Authors find LLMs mostly do not know what they know, so verification without tools is unreliable.
limits: Needs tool access; gains differ by task.
agent_relevance: Supports G2/G3: tool output as the critique. S5 should be fed execution results.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR)
finding: On HumanEval and APPS, once repair cost is counted, self-repair gains are modest, vary, or vanish. The bottleneck is feedback quality.
numbers: GPT-4 on APPS: 10 initial samples then 1 repair each (up to 20) gives 1.05x the pass rate of pass@20; 2 initial samples then 10 repairs each (up to 22) gives 0.97x of pass@22. GPT-3.5 gains only at the largest sample counts; GPT-4 beats baseline by up to 8 points. Stronger-model or human feedback gives much larger gains.
limits: Code only: Code Llama, GPT-3.5, GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Equal-token comparison (G7): spend on diverse initial attempts, then repair little. Matches S3 before S5.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning (NeurIPS)
finding: After a failed episode the agent writes a verbal reflection stored in memory and used next episode. No weight updates.
numbers: Absolute gains: ALFWorld +22% in 12 steps, HotPotQA +20%, HumanEval up to +11% (91% pass@1 vs GPT-4 80%).
limits: Relies on environment feedback or unit tests as the failure signal. Huang et al. note oracle stopping inflates such results.
agent_relevance: The agent-loop form of S5/S9: failure signal from a real check, one-line lesson, retry. Fits the schema when the signal is code-made.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs (COLM)
finding: Models correct an injected error placed in the user turn but not the identical error in their own output. Appending the word Wait nearly removes the gap.
numbers: 14 open-source non-reasoning models: 64.5% average blind spot. Fine-tuning on 5,306 error-correction traces cuts it by 76.0%. Appending Wait cuts it by 89.3% without training. Confirmed on closed frontier models and on logic and object tracking.
limits: Injected errors, not always natural ones. Non-reasoning models; reasoning models close part of the gap.
agent_relevance: A free trigger-time prompt (Wait). Also supports presenting the failing output to a fresh context as if external (S3 isolation, S5 framing).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet - cost and prompt confounds
finding: Earlier gains also came from weak first prompts. On CommonGen-Hard, the prior paper reports 44.0 standard vs 67.0 self-correct. With an informative first prompt, the baseline rises and self-correction adds little or loses.
numbers: Table 8 (as extracted): prior-paper rows 44.0 vs 67.0; re-test rows 53.0 vs 61.1 and 81.8 vs 75.1 (standard vs self-correct, with the best first prompt giving 81.8 against 75.1 after correction).
limits: Row labels from text extraction; read as direction of effect, not exact cell identities. Small set of tasks.
agent_relevance: Always compare to a strong first prompt at equal tokens (G7). Our plain-model baseline must carry the full instructions.

source: Lee et al. (2025) ReVISE - headline claims and transfer limits
finding: The introduction headline uses Maj@3 gains. Out-of-domain transfer is much weaker than in-domain. The authors admit stage-2 correction training lowers verification accuracy.
numbers: Intro: GSM8K 27.1 -> 31.1 (Maj@3, Llama3 1B), MATH 33.2 -> 36.0 (Maj@3, Llama3 8B). Transfer (Table 4): 8.8% on Llama-3.2-1B and 61.5% on Llama-3.1-8B GSM8K accuracy when trained on another domain.
limits: Headline Maj@3 differs from Table 1 (Maj@5). No independent replication found.
agent_relevance: The trigger is reliable only inside the trained domain; out of domain it is a guess.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench - cause analysis
finding: The blind spot is traced to post-training data: supervised fine-tuning sets hold near-zero error-correction sequences, while reasoning-model training data holds far more. Steering along a conversational-role direction activates correction.
numbers: LoRA fine-tune, two epochs, 5,306 correction traces: blind spot down 76.0%. Wait token: down 89.3%, through a nearly independent pathway from the role direction. Mechanistic test in two model families at 7B to 8B.
limits: Mechanistic result only at 7B to 8B in two families; behavior gap seen in all 14 models.
agent_relevance: Explains why untrained prompts fail to revise own output (Huang) and why trained triggers such as ReVISE can work. For us: reframe own output as external evidence before S5.
